label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: Each member woke at its own minute, did one step of its queue with its reviews, and closed.
findings.why: Wakes, queue and reviews are used as if known; as a first reader setting up a small newsroom I cannot yet picture what a wake is or what its reviews are.

findings.quote: The conductor set the pace and wrote the night log's third edition. Deck sent its second experiment to ruv-sgit
findings.why: A run of short sentences each naming a member and a job, with deck, ruv-sgit and the night log all unexplained, reads as a list and loses me.

findings.quote: What the record shows is not whether everything finished, but whether what did not finish was written down
findings.why: This is the most useful idea for my own newsroom, but it is told as what the record shows rather than as what I learned or would now look for.

findings.quote: Part four keeps all three, and asks what that order should have been.
findings.why: It points ahead to an order of stages I have not been told about, so I stall wondering what the right order was.

findings.quote: the second time in the day that one member's decision became a setting every member's work must pass
findings.why: One very long, dense paragraph of gate checks, type scales and a table mixes three topics; I skim it and lose the point about the designer owning its mistake.

findings.quote: A piece marked ready for me, then another. A list of what waits on me, refreshed every hour.
findings.why: Fragments stacked three deep, and the queue idea is told again at lines 166 and 168.

findings.quote: everything it had made was waiting on me. Minutes later deck passed the third version
findings.why: ruv-sgit's line at 166 already says everything is waiting on him, and the narrator then says it again, and the closing summary at 180 says it a third time.

findings.quote: Nine hours. Every wake started by the clock. Every wake with its five stages.
findings.why: The closing paragraph re-lists every scene of the chapter in staccato form, so a reader who has just read them gets them a second time.

findings.quote: The team is temporary. The record is not. And the record is what the next factory is built from.
findings.why: Three short sentences in a row on the chapter's key idea, which reads as a slogan, though the idea itself is the one I most want.

findings.quote: This is this book's conductor, not the talk's, and this book's storyteller and researcher too
findings.why: Two teams, two conductors and a handover are introduced in one sentence before I have met either team, and I stop following who is who.

findings.quote: I want to show you the rest of that handover, because it is one of the most useful documents in this part of the book
findings.why: It tells me in advance that the document is useful instead of letting me find out, a mild ranking of the reader's attention.

findings.quote: Writing the handover you would want today is a good test of yours.
findings.why: The card gives an instruction on what to do and then judges it a good test, where my own newsroom would need a concrete first step.

findings.quote: Hey, I'm this book's conductor. The schedule, the keys and the decisions.
findings.why: Twelve self-introductions in the same 'Hey, I'm' shape with the same one-line job form a long catalogue, and for a newsroom builder the table at line 45 then repeats it.

findings.quote: You do not need all of these to start.
findings.why: This is exactly my question, but it is answered with one flat line and the useful answer (three members) is held out of print, so I am left with twelve roles and no starting point.

findings.quote: The order of the times was right. The order of the work was not.
findings.why: The historian's paragraph is a tangle of first pages, merges and parallel work on dev and the conductor, and the lesson at 118 only lands after I have lost the thread.

what_holds: 09-nine-hours-with-nobody-starting-work.md: the partial wakes that say so (line 26 to 30) and the empty mailroom (line 164 to 168) are exactly the evidence a would-be editor wants, and the morning review that ends with what only the editor can decide (line 85 to 89) is a pattern I would copy.

20-sessions-end.md: 'A session is not a member' is the clearest idea in the three sections, and the walk through the handover headings (line 65 to 73) is something I could copy for my own agents on the day.

21-the-second-factory.md: the failures told in each member's own words, and the brake line corrected by the researcher, show a team that checks its editor; the table of commits and wakes tells me what a second team costs.
notes: Taken together the three sections speak to my question, whether agents could run my newsroom while I sign, and the answer from chapter 9 (a queue only the editor can clear) is honest. The main stalls are vocabulary that is used before it is explained (wake, gate, five stages, pre-review) and the amount of book-internal history in chapters 20 and 21, for example two teams with two conductors, that I do not need to start. Chapter 21 lines 11, 64, 88, 104 and 106 are team notes and were skipped as a reader would.
